list.listitem: Consider cutaneous larva migrans in patients with pruritic, reddish brown, serpiginous lesions that advance several millimeters per day and primarily involve the feet, legs, and buttocks. C
Obtain travel history pertaining to exposure to potentially contaminated soil or sand, particularly in warmer climates. C
Symptoms are generally benign and self-limited but can be very uncomfortable and may persist for weeks to months. C
Treatment of choice is oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg × 1 dose. One or two additional doses can be given if rash is not resolved with single-dose therapy. C

background.definition: Cutaneous larva migrans is one of the most common tropically acquired dermatoses, typically caused by the infective-stage larvae of the dog or cat hookworm. The organisms penetrate and migrate in human skin, producing an inflammatory reaction, referred to as creeping eruptions, along the cutaneous tract of their migration. Pulmonary and visceral involvement, although rare, have been reported.

list.listitem: Exact incidence is unknown, but one study reported that 6.7% of 13,300 travelers visiting a travel-related disease clinic presented with cutaneous larva migrans.

Incidence may be higher in endemic areas, most commonly Africa, the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America. Cases have also been reported in warm climates in other countries, including the United States (eg, Florida).
The disease is most commonly caused by larvae of the dog or cat hookworm, Ancylostoma braziliense. It may also be caused by other animal hookworms.
Disease is caused by exposure to contaminated soil or sand in warm areas (eg, playground sandbox, beach).
Skin comes into contact with contaminated sand/soil containing infective-stage larvae, which are hatched in warmer climates from eggs passed in dog or cat feces.
Larvae penetrate the skin, usually of the feet, legs, and buttocks/anogenital region, resulting in a pruritic, erythematous papule at the entry site.
Several days to weeks later, pruritic, serpiginous, reddish-brown elevated tracts appear as larvae migrate in skin, where they die and become absorbed.
Humans are incidental hosts in which larvae cannot complete their life cycle.

Prevention involves hookworm testing and treatment for pet dogs and cats. Stray animals should be reported to animal control, and animal feces should be removed promptly from areas of human activity. C
Diagnosis is clinical. Stool and serological studies are often unnecessary. C
Obtain travel history and any history pertaining to exposure to potentially contaminated soil or sand, particularly in warmer climates. C
Differentiate lesions of CLM from rashes that may appear similar such as rashes seen in Strongyloides infection, scabies, and Lyme disease. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Pulmonary and GI symptoms are not uncommon; tract of larval migration proceeds significantly faster; symptoms may wax and wane over time
Potential exposure to mites, crusted lesions, interdigital web involvement, microscopic visualization of Sarcoptes scabiei
Annular lesions with central clearing that are generally located near axilla, inguinal region, behind knees, at belt line (corresponding to ticks feeding in moist regions of body, along skin folds)

list.listitem: A major risk factor is exposure to potentially contaminated sand or soil in a warm climate.

Patients typically present with pruritus (98%), reddish brown serpiginous raised tracts (97%), localized swelling (17%), and pain (10%). Other symptoms may include papulovesicles and pustules (10%). Rash may develop several days to several weeks after exposure and progresses at a rate of several millimeters per day.
Lesions are commonly found on the lower extremities (73.4% of all locations), buttocks/anogential region (13%), trunk, and upper extremities (each 7%).
Laboratory findings (eg, stool examination, serologic testing) are not helpful in establishing the diagnosis.
If pulmonary involvement is suspected, definitive diagnosis requires recovery of larvae from respiratory secretions. However, this is rarely needed, as the disease is generally self-limited.

Suspect cutaneous larva migrans in patients presenting with a history of potential exposure (eg, recent travel to a tropical location or exposure to warm moist soil or sand that is potentially contaminated with dog or cat feces) and characteristic skin lesions.

A presumptive diagnosis of pulmonary involvement is made when respiratory symptoms accompany the cutaneous lesions. Definitive diagnosis (usually not needed because the symptoms are self-limited) is made when larvae are recovered from respiratory secretions or bronchoalveolar lavage.
Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg × 1 dose is reported to have a cure rate of 77%. Consider 1 or 2 additional doses if not resolved. C
Alternative treatment is oral albendazole 200 mg twice daily for 3 to 5 days. C
Topical thiabendazole applied 2 to 3 times daily for 5 days may also be effective. C
Reevaluate patient if skin lesions do not resolve after 1 to 2 weeks of treatment. Additional doses of an antihelminthic drug may be needed. C

Oral ivermectin 200 mcg/kg × 1 dose is reported to have a cure rate of 77%, with mean resolution of pruritus and lesions in 3 and 9 days, respectively. Cure rate increases to 97% with additional 1 or 2 doses of ivermectin.
Ivermectin is safe in children weighing less than 15 kg, based on a systematic review of 15 studies with over 1000 participants.

A study of 44 patients found that 24 of 31 (77%) who received oral albendazole 200 mg twice daily for 3 days were cured. One week of daily oral albendazole 400 mg showed a 100% cure rate in 78 patients after 3 months of follow-up.
While not FDA approved, topical thiabendazole 10% to 15% cream applied 2 to 3 times daily for 5 to 10 days has a reported cure rate of 80% to 98% in small series.

Thiabendazole is not commercially available as a topical formulation, but a water-soluble base can be made containing crushed 500 mg thiabendazole tablets. Successful topical use of 10% to 15% oral suspensions has also been reported.
Surgery is not recommended, as larva are situated 1 to 2 cm ahead of the visible track and cannot be localized reliably. Also, surgery or cryotherapy can result in undesirable cosmetic outcomes.
The main complications are secondary infection or allergic reaction, but these are relatively uncommon.
Rarely, larvae spread hematogenously to the lungs, resulting in a nonproductive cough that typically lasts less than 2 weeks but has been reported to persist for up to 9 months.
Prognosis is excellent, as humans are “dead-end hosts.” Lesions generally resolve untreated in several days to weeks, but some lesions may recur and last for nine months or more. C
Treatment with antihelminthic agents may reduce the risk of secondary bacterial infection, and substantially reduces duration of symptoms, such as severe pruritus. C
